name: Facing Hard Things
tagline: Meeting what happens to you — disappointment, fear, failure, loss — with honesty, courage, and recovery. Prerequisites here are suggestions; character grows in a spiral.

skills.name: Name what you're feeling
skills.gotItWhen: When something's going on inside you, you can find a word for it — angry, embarrassed, jealous, left out, worried — and say it out loud to someone, or at least to yourself.
looksLike: You stomp upstairs, and later you can say 'I was embarrassed, not just mad.'
Before a tryout you notice 'this is nerves' and can tell the difference between nerves and dread.
A friend gets the thing you wanted, and you can admit — at least to yourself — that it's jealousy, and that jealousy is survivable.
waysToBuild: Use a feelings wheel at dinner: everyone names their day's biggest feeling, parents included.
After a blowup has cooled, do the replay: what was the feeling under the behavior?
Keep a one-line journal for a couple of weeks: today's strongest feeling, one word.

skills.name: Settle yourself down
skills.gotItWhen: When your body floods — heart pounding, face hot, tears or fury rising — you have ways that work to bring yourself back to steady, and you reach for them yourself.
looksLike: You feel the surge coming in an argument and step out to breathe before you say the thing.
After a scary near-miss on your bike, you get yourself breathing slow again before riding on.
You know your own early-warning signs — clenched jaw, hot face — and treat them as the signal to act.
waysToBuild: Find your two go-to tools (slow breathing, cold water, walking, counting) by testing them when you're calm.
Agree on a family 'pause' signal anyone can use — including you, on yourself.
After the next flood, note what worked, what didn't, and what you'd try sooner.

skills.name: Wait well
skills.gotItWhen: When there's a gap between wanting and getting — a line, a countdown, a slow answer, a someday — you can hold the wait with patience and even make something of it, keeping your good mood and your good behavior intact.
looksLike: The road trip is long, the tablet is dead, and you find a way to be decent company anyway.
Your birthday is weeks out; you're excited without being unbearable about it.
The answer is 'we'll see,' and you can live inside 'we'll see' without reopening it hourly.
waysToBuild: Practice tiny waits on purpose: dessert after everyone's served, opening the package after dinner.
On the next long wait, bring nothing — and see what your head finds to do.
Save the best part of something (last chapter, last bite) deliberately, just to feel the muscle work.

skills.name: Do it scared
skills.gotItWhen: When something worth doing frightens you — the audition, the phone call, the high dive, the new group — you can feel the fear fully and go anyway, because you've learned fear is information, not a stop sign.
looksLike: Your hand is shaking when you knock on the neighbor's door to ask for the job — and you knock.
You sign up for the solo, spend a week nervous, and sing it.
First day at a new team practice: you walk in alone, heart going, and introduce yourself.
waysToBuild: Keep a 'did it scared' list — every entry is proof for the next one.
Pick one small scary thing a week for a month; size doesn't matter, going does.
Learn your own pattern: is the fear worst before, during, or after? (It's almost always before.)

skills.name: Ask for help
skills.gotItWhen: When you're stuck, hurting, or in over your head, you can go to the right person and say what's actually going on — because you've learned that asking is a strength move, and that carrying it alone is the riskier choice.
looksLike: You're drowning in a class and tell the teacher before the grade does the telling.
Something happened online that scares you, and you bring it to a parent even though it's awkward.
You watch a friend struggle alone and realize you'd never want to be that stuck — so you don't let yourself be.
waysToBuild: Name your people: for each kind of trouble (school, friends, scary stuff), who's your first call?
Practice the opening line — 'I need help with something' — until it's boring to say.
Watch how the adults you respect ask for help, and notice how often they do.

skills.name: Take feedback
skills.gotItWhen: When someone tells you something you did could be better — a coach, a teacher, a parent, a friend — you can hear them out, look for the true part, and thank them, even when it stings and even when they said it clumsily.
looksLike: Your coach corrects your form in front of everyone; you nod, try it their way, and it's better.
An essay comes back covered in red; after the first wave of ugh, you read every comment.
A friend says you've been kind of a lot lately — and instead of firing back, you ask what they mean.
waysToBuild: Ask for feedback on purpose once a week — 'what's one thing I could do better?' — from someone who'll be honest.
Practice the two-step: say 'tell me more' before you say anything else.
Sort a real piece of criticism into true / partly true / not true, on paper, after the sting fades.

skills.name: Lose well
skills.gotItWhen: When you lose — the game, the election, the part, the argument — you can congratulate the winner and mean at least half of it, feel the disappointment honestly, and be someone people still want to play with tomorrow.
looksLike: You lose the board game on the last turn and shake your head, laugh, and set up the next round.
Someone else gets the part you wanted; you tell them congratulations before you go feel your feelings.
Your team gets crushed and you're the one who keeps the sideline from turning sour.
waysToBuild: Play more games you might lose — losing practice only comes from losing.
Adopt a losing ritual: handshake, one honest sentence about the disappointment, done.
Watch how your favorite athletes lose, and steal from the ones who do it well.

skills.name: Try again after it goes wrong
skills.gotItWhen: When an honest attempt fails — the tryout, the test, the recipe, the plan — you can absorb the miss, figure out what it taught you, and take another real swing instead of quietly retiring from the thing.
looksLike: You get cut from the team, cry about it, and start planning for next season's tryout.
The cake comes out flat; the second cake happens the same week.
You bomb a test, find out what went wrong, and show up different for the next one.
waysToBuild: After a miss, write the two-line report: what happened, what changes next time.
Tell the story of a failure at dinner and let the family cheer the retry, not the result.
Pick one abandoned thing you quietly quit and give it one honest second attempt.

skills.name: Be okay with nothing to do
skills.gotItWhen: When there's empty time and no screen to fill it, you can settle into it and let it be — and more often than not, the boredom turns into something: an idea, a project, a wander, a rest you needed.
looksLike: The wifi is down and within the hour you're building something, reading something, or outside.
You wait at a restaurant with no phone and manage to just… be there, maybe even talk.
You've learned that your best ideas show up about ten minutes into being bored, so you let it run.
waysToBuild: Do a screen-free stretch every week — long enough to get past the itchy part.
Keep a 'bored list' of things you always wish you had time for, posted where boredom strikes.
Sit somewhere with literally nothing for a while, and just watch what your brain does.

skills.name: Roll with changed plans
skills.gotItWhen: When the thing you were counting on changes — the trip's canceled, the friend bails, the rain comes — you can absorb the hit, adjust, and find what's still good in the day that actually happened.
looksLike: The beach day gets rained out and you're part of inventing the backup plan, not the storm cloud over it.
A friend cancels last minute; you're disappointed out loud once, then you make other plans.
The order comes out wrong at the restaurant and you either fix it politely or shrug and eat.
waysToBuild: Have a parent 'change the plan' on purpose sometimes, small stakes, and debrief after.
Build the family reflex of asking 'okay — what's plan B?' out loud, together.
After a real derailment, name one thing that turned out fine, or better, because of it.

skills.name: Own your mistakes
skills.gotItWhen: When you've done the wrong thing — broken it, said it, forgotten it — you can say so plainly and let the confession stand on its own, apologize like you mean it, and take a real step to repair the damage.
looksLike: You broke the window playing ball inside, and you're the one who tells them, before they find it.
Your apology names what you did — 'I read your messages, that was wrong' — not 'sorry you're upset.'
You forgot your part of the group project, say so to the group, and take the worst remaining job.
waysToBuild: Learn the three-part repair: what I did, what it cost you, what I'll do about it.
Watch for the excuse reflex — 'but you' / 'it's just' — and practice cutting a confession off before it turns.
Notice how the adults you trust apologize, and hold the family to it both directions — parents owe kids real apologies too.

skills.name: Take no for an answer
skills.gotItWhen: When a decision goes against you and it's not yours to make, you can hear the no, make your case once — calmly, if it really matters — and then genuinely accept the answer and stay warm with the person who gave it.
looksLike: The answer to the sleepover is no; you make one real argument, hear the reasons, and let it go — actually go.
The coach benches you for the big game and you stay on the sideline cheering.
You're told the concert's out of budget, and the rest of the evening isn't a hostage situation.
waysToBuild: Learn the 'one appeal' rule: everyone gets one calm, well-argued appeal — and then the answer stands.
After a no you took well, have a parent tell you they noticed; after one you didn't, replay it cold.
Watch what campaigning after a no does to trust — and what accepting one does.

skills.name: Choose hard on purpose
skills.gotItWhen: You sometimes pick the harder thing when the easy one was right there — the cold water, the long route, the heavy chore, the early morning — because you've learned that deliberately chosen discomfort makes the unchosen kind smaller.
looksLike: You take the stairs, the cold shower, the heavy end of the couch — small, chosen, regularly.
You sign up for the harder class or the longer race knowing exactly what you're signing up for.
When real hardship shows up uninvited, part of you recognizes it: you've trained in this weather.
waysToBuild: Adopt one small chosen hardship for a month and keep it privately — no announcing.
Do a family hard thing — a long hike, a fast, a dawn start — and talk after about what it built.
Notice the moment of the flinch, and practice stepping toward instead of away.

skills.name: Face a fear that's been chasing you
skills.gotItWhen: You can pick a fear that's actually been shaping your choices — the dog, the deep end, the speaking up, the dark — walk toward it on purpose, in steps, and shrink it until it no longer decides things for you.
looksLike: You've been quietly routing around dogs for years; this season, you learn to greet one.
The deep end has kept you at the shallow rope; you work the ladder of it until you're jumping in.
You realize you never raise your hand because of one bad moment in third grade — and you retire that rule.
waysToBuild: Name your top fear honestly, then build a ladder: the tiniest version of facing it, up to the real thing.
Take one rung a week, with someone you trust who knows what you're doing.
Keep the before-and-after note: what the fear used to cost you, and what it costs now.

skills.name: Stand alone
skills.gotItWhen: When the group is moving toward something you know is wrong — the shoplifting dare, the pile-on, the cruel joke, the party plan — you can hold your ground, say your no out loud, and stay or leave with your own mind intact, even at the cost of belonging.
looksLike: Everyone's mocking the new kid in the group chat, and your message is the one that doesn't join.
The dare is to take something small from the store; your 'nah, I'm out' costs you some cool and you pay it.
At a sleepover the video everyone wants to watch crosses your line, and you actually leave the room.
waysToBuild: Decide your lines before you need them — it's a hundred times easier than deciding under pressure.
Rehearse two exit lines that work at your school and don't sound preachy.
Set up a no-questions-asked extraction code with your parents, and know it will be honored.

skills.name: Let yourself grieve
skills.gotItWhen: When you lose something that mattered — a pet, a friendship, a grandparent, a big hope — you can let the sadness be real and let it take the time it takes, keep talking to your people through it, and carry the loss as a true part of your story.
looksLike: The dog dies and you cry, tell stories about her, and don't apologize for either.
Your best friend moves away and you let it hurt — and you say so instead of going quiet.
Months after a loss, a wave hits out of nowhere, and you've learned that waves are how it works.
waysToBuild: When loss comes, mark it — a burial, a photo book, a letter — rituals give grief somewhere to stand.
Keep one open conversation going with a parent through a real loss, even just minutes at a time.
Learn the family's stories of grief: who was lost, how it felt, what helped.

skills.name: Stay steady when everything goes sideways
skills.gotItWhen: When something genuinely goes wrong around you — blood, a crash, a fire alarm that isn't a drill, a lost little kid — you can keep your head, do the next useful thing, and get the right help moving, becoming part of the response instead of part of the scene.
looksLike: Your sibling gashes a knee and you're the one getting pressure on it and calling for a parent.
The kitchen pan flares up and you remember: lid, not water.
A little kid is lost and crying at the park; you stay with them and flag down the right adult.
waysToBuild: Learn what to do *before* you need it — first aid basics buy calm in the moment.
Run family drills seriously enough that your body knows the way out.
After any real scare, debrief it: what did you do, what would you do sooner next time?

skills.name: Bounce back from embarrassment
skills.gotItWhen: After a public faceplant — the wrong note, the tripped entrance, the mispronounced word everyone caught — you can feel the burn, keep your sense of humor about yourself, and get back into the room, the game, or the group without letting the moment write the story.
looksLike: Your voice cracks in the presentation; you grin, say 'well then,' and finish the presentation.
You call the teacher 'mom' and survive the laughter — laughing along is what disarms it.
A week after the cafeteria trip-and-spill, you're eating in the cafeteria, not the library.
waysToBuild: Collect the family's most embarrassing stories and notice: everyone has them, everyone lived.
Learn the recovery line — a small joke at your own expense — and keep one loaded.
After a burn, apply the ten-year test: will this matter in ten years? Will anyone else even remember it in ten days?

skills.name: Keep hope in a hard season
skills.gotItWhen: When a hard stretch drags on — the injury, the friendless semester, the family crisis — you can be honest about how bad it is and still hold on to the belief, out loud, that this is a season and not the whole story, and act like someone with a future.
looksLike: Months into the injury, you're honest that it stinks — and you're still doing the rehab.
In a lonely stretch at a new school you keep showing up to things, because 'not yet' isn't 'never.'
When the family's in a hard patch, you can say both true things: this is heavy, and we've gotten through heavy before.
waysToBuild: Keep a record of past hard seasons and how they ended — your own evidence file for hope.
Learn to say both halves in one sentence: 'this is really hard, and it won't always be like this.'
Find the people and practices (prayer, a mentor, a team) that hold hope for you when you can't.

skills.name: Walk through a real trial
skills.gotItWhen: Life has handed you something genuinely hard — a real loss, a real failure, a real long valley — and you walked through it, not around it: you felt it honestly, asked for help, kept going, and came out the other side someone who knows they can do hard things, because they have.
looksLike: The year everything went wrong — and you can tell the story now: what broke, who helped, what grew.
You went through the thing you'd have said you couldn't handle, and you handled it.
A friend hits their own valley, and you're the one who knows the terrain.
waysToBuild: This one can't be scheduled — the trial finds you. Everything else in this lane is training for it.
When you're in it, use it all: name it, settle, ask for help, grieve, hold hope.
When you're through, tell the story somewhere it counts — the family table, a journal, a younger kid who needs it.
